purpose: Extend the trade-catalogue analysis from printed offerings and circulation events to surviving material endpoints.

principal_findings.printed_anchor: Bourgogne's 1862 catalogue is already treated in the trade matrix as evidence for quality grades, formats and prices of microscopic preparations.
principal_findings.surviving_endpoint: National Museum of American History preserves a boxed set of microscope slides inscribed BOURGOGNE; the museum attributes the inscription probably to Joseph Bourgogne.
principal_findings.new_chain: priced/graded trade catalogue → named commercial maker → later surviving boxed set
principal_findings.current_limit: The public object record does not expose a row-level transcription of subjects, catalogue numbers, grades, or original purchase provenance. Catalogue-to-object identity remains unclosed until the slides and labels are transcribed.
principal_findings.next_action: Request or derive high-resolution label/subject transcription for the NMAH set and compare against the 1862 catalogue row schema.
principal_findings.priority: A+ because the physical endpoint already exists and the printed catalogue is already in the corpus

principal_findings.printed_anchor: The bibliography and trade/technical corpus already include nineteenth-century test-plate and microscopical-ruling literature, including Australian Grayson material and references to Nobert/Möller standards.
principal_findings.surviving_endpoint: NMAH preserves an 1884 Charles Fasoldt test slide and glass-plate photomicrographs produced from a Nobert nineteen-band test plate; the museum reconstructs Barnard's 1867 acquisition and Woodward/Curtis observations in 1868–1869.
principal_findings.new_chain: precision-made test slide → acquisition → microscope-resolution experiment → photomicrographic derivative → publication/dispute → museum object
principal_findings.research_payoff: This establishes a second commodity/object regime distinct from specimen preparations. The slide is a metrological standard whose value lies in repeatable optical difficulty rather than biological identity.
principal_findings.comparison_to_trade_slides: Bourgogne/Cole preparations ask what specimen can be seen and interpreted; test plates ask what the microscope can resolve. Both circulate as glass objects, but their epistemic work and valuation criteria differ.

revised_trade_argument.previous: catalogue → price/package → retail → exhibition/society use → exchange → second-hand resale
revised_trade_argument.expanded: catalogue → price/package → retail → use/exhibition → exchange/resale → surviving object → modern recataloguing
revised_trade_argument.claim: Trade catalogues are most analytically powerful when treated as one address system among several. A priced catalogue names an object as a commodity; a surviving museum record names it as a collection object. The research problem is to recover the crosswalk between those identities.

object_first_extraction_rule: For every named maker already present in the trade matrix, search current museum databases for surviving sets before adding more general trade literature.
Prioritize boxed or numbered sets because order can preserve catalogue or series structure.
Do not infer that a museum set was purchased from the exact catalogue edition merely because maker and subject match.
Transcribe labels verbatim before normalizing taxon, anatomy, locality, or maker names.
Preserve museum accession and catalogue numbers separately from historical maker/catalogue numbers.
